microtopics.title: Classify after putting the equation in standard form
microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The first has every rational; the second has none. The reduced constant comparison matters when the coefficient is zero.

teaching_path.why_valid: Adding 2x to both complete sides preserves equality.
inputs: Over the rationals, classify 3x − 4 = 1 − 2x as having no solution, one solution, or every rational as a solution. Use the criterion Ax = B: A nonzero gives one rational solution, A = B = 0 gives every rational, and A = 0 with B nonzero gives none. Do not report the value of x.

teaching_path.why_valid: Adding 4 to both sides is reversible.
The coefficient 5 is nonzero, so exactly one rational can satisfy the equation.
One counterexample suffices to refute that every rational works.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Any linear-looking equation has every rational as a solution.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Classify 4x+1=4x+1 and 4x+1=4x+2. Do not solve by dividing by the cancelled coefficient.
misconceptions.repair: The first has every rational; the second has none. The reduced constant comparison matters when the coefficient is zero.

exit_task.prompt: Classify 4x+1=4x+1 and 4x+1=4x+2. Do not solve by dividing by the cancelled coefficient.

answer.summary: The first has every rational; the second has none. The reduced constant comparison matters when the coefficient is zero.
reasoning: The first has every rational; the second has none. The reduced constant comparison matters when the coefficient is zero.
answer.check: Classify 7x+2=7x+3. Expected: no solution, because it reduces to 2=3.

microtopics.title: Classify linked parameter exceptions
microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: At t=3 every rational works; at t=4 exactly one works. Split a zero divisor before cancelling.

teaching_path.why_valid: Distribution and subtracting the same term from both sides preserve the solution set.
inputs: Let k be rational and x rational. For each k, classify each of these equations as having none, one, or every rational solution: E1: 2(x−3)=2x+k; E2: (k−2)x=4−2k. Use the Ax=B criteria; a numerical solution is not requested.

teaching_path.why_valid: The reduced statement has no x, so it holds for all x or for none.
teaching_path.output: Every rational if k=−6; none otherwise.

inputs: Every rational if k=−6; none otherwise.

teaching_path.why_valid: At k=2 both sides vanish; division by k−2 would lose this case.
teaching_path.output: E2 has every rational if k=2.

teaching_path.why_valid: A nonzero rational coefficient has a unique rational quotient.
inputs: E2 has every rational if k=2.
teaching_path.output: E2 has one rational solution for k≠2.

teaching_path.why_valid: Each category must be evaluated in the original pair.
inputs: E2 has one rational solution for k≠2.
teaching_path.output: At k=−6: E1 every, E2 one. At k=2: E1 none, E2 every.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Cancelling a parameter factor is valid even where the factor is zero.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Classify (t−3)y=2(t−3) at t=3 and t=4, keeping the exceptional case.
misconceptions.repair: At t=3 every rational works; at t=4 exactly one works. Split a zero divisor before cancelling.

exit_task.prompt: Classify (t−3)y=2(t−3) at t=3 and t=4, keeping the exceptional case.

answer.summary: At t=3 every rational works; at t=4 exactly one works. Split a zero divisor before cancelling.
reasoning: At t=3 every rational works; at t=4 exactly one works. Split a zero divisor before cancelling.
answer.check: Classify (t+1)y=3(t+1). Expected: every rational at t=−1; one otherwise.

microtopics.title: Classify with a coupled domain boundary
microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: At a=2 the equation is defined but inconsistent (no solution); at a=3 exactly one rational works; at a=2+√2 the sole real candidate 1/√2 is irrational, so no rational works. Domain checks come after valid branch reduction.

teaching_path.action: Exclude the parameter making the second equation undefined.
teaching_path.why_valid: Its right denominator k−2 must be nonzero.
inputs: Extension beyond routine linear equations. k is real, x must be rational. Classify the simultaneous system by k as INVALID PARAMETER, NO RATIONAL SOLUTION, ONE RATIONAL SOLUTION, or EVERY RATIONAL SOLUTION: (k−1)(k−2)x=k−1 and (x+1)/(x−1)=k/(k−2). An equation with a zero denominator is invalid; a solution must satisfy both original equations and x≠1. Report categories and the parameter cases, not a general numerical solution method.

teaching_path.why_valid: The first equation then reads 0=0, while the second remains defined.
teaching_path.output: The second becomes (x+1)/(x−1)=−1, giving x=0; it is rational and allowed.

teaching_path.action: Reduce the first equation for k outside {1,2}.
teaching_path.why_valid: Only in this branch is cancellation of k−1 followed by division by k−2 valid.
inputs: The second becomes (x+1)/(x−1)=−1, giving x=0; it is rational and allowed.

teaching_path.action: Reduce the second equation with both denominator conditions retained.
teaching_path.why_valid: Cross-multiplication is reversible when x≠1 and k≠2.

teaching_path.action: Require the two candidates to coincide.
teaching_path.why_valid: Both original equations must hold for the same x.
The only compatibility parameters (3±√5)/2 are irrational; x=k−1 is then irrational and excluded.
teaching_path.output: No rational solution for every k outside {1,2}.

teaching_path.action: Verify the exceptional allowed branch in the originals.
teaching_path.why_valid: A reduced-line result is insufficient when divisions were used in other branches.
inputs: No rational solution for every k outside {1,2}.
teaching_path.output: k=1,x=0 gives 0=0 and 1/(−1)=1/(−1). ONE at k=1; INVALID at k=2; NONE otherwise; never EVERY.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: A real solution found after cancelling is automatically an allowed rational solution.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Let y be rational and a real. Classify (a−2)y=1 at a=2, a=3 and a=2+√2. Keep undefined operations separate from empty solution sets.
misconceptions.repair: At a=2 the equation is defined but inconsistent (no solution); at a=3 exactly one rational works; at a=2+√2 the sole real candidate 1/√2 is irrational, so no rational works. Domain checks come after valid branch reduction.

exit_task.prompt: Let y be rational and a real. Classify (a−2)y=1 at a=2, a=3 and a=2+√2. Keep undefined operations separate from empty solution sets.

answer.summary: At a=2 the equation is defined but inconsistent (no solution); at a=3 exactly one rational works; at a=2+√2 the sole real candidate 1/√2 is irrational, so no rational works. Domain checks come after valid branch reduction.
reasoning: At a=2 the equation is defined but inconsistent (no solution); at a=3 exactly one rational works; at a=2+√2 the sole real candidate 1/√2 is irrational, so no rational works. Domain checks come after valid branch reduction.
answer.check: Change the unknown domain to real. Expected: one solution also at k=(3±√5)/2; k=1 remains one, k=2 invalid, all other k none.

independent_checks.statement: At k=1, x=0 satisfies both originals. At k=2 a denominator is zero. At the two real compatibility roots, x is irrational, so a real solution does not meet the rational-domain request.

microtopics.title: Execute an inverse chain across a table and a process graph
microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: These are the same observation. Both give B=8, A=4/3 and X=11/3 cm. Different results reveal a unit mapping error.

teaching_path.why_valid: Ten millimetres are one centimetre.
inputs: A measuring program uses numerical readings in centimetres: X → A=(X−1)/2 → B=3A+4 → C=(B+2)/5. The observation table gives C=22 millimetres. The inverse procedure is prescribed: convert the observation to centimetres, undo the C operation, then B, then A. Execute it to recover X and verify every forward stage. Treat the displayed readings as exact.

teaching_path.why_valid: Multiplication by nonzero 5 and subtraction of 2 reverse this stage.
Subtract 4, then divide by nonzero 3.
Multiply by nonzero 2, then add 1.
A correct recovered input must reproduce the original observation after every named operation.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: The table number can be substituted directly although the program uses a different unit.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Run the same inverse program with C=20 millimetres, and separately with C=2 centimetres. Should X differ?
misconceptions.repair: These are the same observation. Both give B=8, A=4/3 and X=11/3 cm. Different results reveal a unit mapping error.

exit_task.prompt: Run the same inverse program with C=20 millimetres, and separately with C=2 centimetres. Should X differ?

answer.summary: These are the same observation. Both give B=8, A=4/3 and X=11/3 cm. Different results reveal a unit mapping error.
reasoning: These are the same observation. Both give B=8, A=4/3 and X=11/3 cm. Different results reveal a unit mapping error.
answer.check: Use C=20 mm. Expected X=11/3 cm; the forward chain gives 2 cm.

microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The first admits every rational, the second none. A rule is selected by both coefficients, not the word linear.

teaching_path.why_valid: The problem explicitly excludes A=0.
inputs: A linear calibration is stated as Ax=B with rational A and B, and A is known to be nonzero. Choose the governing rule for recovering x: R1, x=B/A; R2, infer every rational is a solution from 0=0. Only choose the applicable rule; do not compute a value.

teaching_path.why_valid: Division by the fixed nonzero rational A is defined and reversible.
The all-solutions rule needs A=B=0 and therefore conflicts with the given A≠0.

misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Choose the rule when A=0,B=0, and when A=0,B=1.
misconceptions.repair: The first admits every rational, the second none. A rule is selected by both coefficients, not the word linear.

exit_task.prompt: Choose the rule when A=0,B=0, and when A=0,B=1.

answer.summary: The first admits every rational, the second none. A rule is selected by both coefficients, not the word linear.
reasoning: The first admits every rational, the second none. A rule is selected by both coefficients, not the word linear.
answer.check: For A=0,B=1, neither division by A nor the all-solutions rule applies; use inconsistency 0=1.

microtopics.title: Translate an ordered pair without changing meaning
microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: They give (4,1) and (1,4), distinct points. Coordinate roles are part of the meaning.

teaching_path.action: Map the table headings to coordinate slots.
teaching_path.why_valid: The convention gives the first slot to x and the second to y.
inputs: The ordered-pair table has columns x and y and one row x=2, y=3. Write that row as a point in Cartesian ordered-pair notation. The coordinate convention is horizontal x first and vertical y second; no equation solving is requested.

teaching_path.why_valid: The row assigns x=2 and y=3.
Its first coordinate would claim x=3, contrary to the row.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: An ordered pair may swap its two coordinates without changing the point.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: Translate rows x=4,y=1 and x=1,y=4. Are their points identical?
misconceptions.repair: They give (4,1) and (1,4), distinct points. Coordinate roles are part of the meaning.

exit_task.prompt: Translate rows x=4,y=1 and x=1,y=4. Are their points identical?

answer.summary: They give (4,1) and (1,4), distinct points. Coordinate roles are part of the meaning.
reasoning: They give (4,1) and (1,4), distinct points. Coordinate roles are part of the meaning.

microtopics.title: Order two dependent inverse steps
microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: The first needs subtract 3 then halve; the second halve then subtract 3. The component list is unchanged, but the dependency changes.

teaching_path.why_valid: The doubled quantity already includes the added 3.
inputs: A starting number is first increased by 3 and then doubled, producing 14. You know the inverse components: subtract 3, and halve. Coordinate them into the correct reverse order. State which component must come first and why; do not calculate the starting number.

teaching_path.why_valid: Halving recovers the quantity before doubling, which still contains the added 3.

teaching_path.action: Check the competing order on a changed start.
teaching_path.why_valid: An independent forward/reverse check tests the dependency rather than memorising a rule.
teaching_path.output: Start 2 gives output 10; halve then subtract gives 2, subtract then halve gives 3.5.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Inverse components can be performed in any order.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: For forward double then add 3, which inverse comes first? Compare with forward add 3 then double.
misconceptions.repair: The first needs subtract 3 then halve; the second halve then subtract 3. The component list is unchanged, but the dependency changes.

exit_task.prompt: For forward double then add 3, which inverse comes first? Compare with forward add 3 then double.

answer.summary: The first needs subtract 3 then halve; the second halve then subtract 3. The component list is unchanged, but the dependency changes.
reasoning: The first needs subtract 3 then halve; the second halve then subtract 3. The component list is unchanged, but the dependency changes.
answer.check: Change the forward order to double then add 3. Expected first inverse: subtract 3.

microtopics.title: Give the warrant for a reversible division
microtopics.badge_reason: The steps are memorable as a procedure, which is exactly why the reversibility condition behind them goes unnoticed until it fails.
entry_assumptions: Use the exact declared domains and the stated category/operation conventions.
microtopics.inferential_jump: It becomes 0=0 and admits every real, so the non-reversible step enlarged the solution set. Identical operations need the relevant reversibility condition.

teaching_path.why_valid: The given divisor 2 is nonzero.
inputs: Over the reals, an author concludes x=4 from 2x=8 by dividing both sides by 2. Supply one warrant explaining why the conclusion follows and why the same justification would fail for division by zero. No further equation solving is requested.

teaching_path.action: Connect the operation to its inverse.
teaching_path.why_valid: Multiplying both sides back by 2 restores the same equality.
teaching_path.output: The step is reversible and preserves the solution set, establishing x=4.

teaching_path.why_valid: Division by zero is undefined, so it has no reversible operation of this kind.
inputs: The step is reversible and preserves the solution set, establishing x=4.
teaching_path.output: The warrant cannot license division by zero.

misconceptions.wrong_idea: Doing any identical operation on both sides automatically preserves the solution set.
misconceptions.diagnostic_prompt: From x=1 multiply both sides by zero. Does the resulting equation have exactly the original solution?
misconceptions.repair: It becomes 0=0 and admits every real, so the non-reversible step enlarged the solution set. Identical operations need the relevant reversibility condition.

exit_task.prompt: From x=1 multiply both sides by zero. Does the resulting equation have exactly the original solution?

answer.summary: It becomes 0=0 and admits every real, so the non-reversible step enlarged the solution set. Identical operations need the relevant reversibility condition.
reasoning: It becomes 0=0 and admits every real, so the non-reversible step enlarged the solution set. Identical operations need the relevant reversibility condition.
answer.check: Justify dividing 3x=9 by 3. Expected: nonzero, defined, reversible; multiplying back verifies the argument.

questions.stem: Over the rationals, classify 3x − 4 = 1 − 2x as having no solution, one solution, or every rational as a solution. Use the criterion Ax = B: A nonzero gives one rational solution, A = B = 0 gives every rational, and A = 0 with B nonzero gives none. Do not report the value of x.
conditions: Original calibration practice; independent educational review pending.

reasoning: Collect the variable terms. Adding 2x to both complete sides preserves equality. 5x − 4 = 1
Remove the constant. Adding 4 to both sides is reversible. 5x = 5
Select the category. The coefficient 5 is nonzero, so exactly one rational can satisfy the equation. One solution.
Challenge an all-solutions claim. One counterexample suffices to refute that every rational works. x=0 gives −4 and 1, which differ.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Adding 2x to both complete sides preserves equality.
inputs: Over the rationals, classify 3x − 4 = 1 − 2x as having no solution, one solution, or every rational as a solution. Use the criterion Ax = B: A nonzero gives one rational solution, A = B = 0 gives every rational, and A = 0 with B nonzero gives none. Do not report the value of x.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Adding 4 to both sides is reversible.
The coefficient 5 is nonzero, so exactly one rational can satisfy the equation.
One counterexample suffices to refute that every rational works.

answer.check: At x=0 the two sides differ, so the category is not every rational. The nonzero coefficient rules out none.

questions.stem: Let k be rational and x rational. For each k, classify each of these equations as having none, one, or every rational solution: E1: 2(x−3)=2x+k; E2: (k−2)x=4−2k. Use the Ax=B criteria; a numerical solution is not requested.
conditions: Original calibration practice; independent educational review pending.

answer.summary: E1: every rational at k=−6, none otherwise. E2: every rational at k=2, one otherwise.
reasoning: Expand E1 and cancel 2x. Distribution and subtracting the same term from both sides preserve the solution set. E1 becomes −6=k.
Classify E1. The reduced statement has no x, so it holds for all x or for none. Every rational if k=−6; none otherwise.
Factor the E2 constant. 4−2k=−2(k−2). (k−2)x=−2(k−2).
Separate k=2 before division. At k=2 both sides vanish; division by k−2 would lose this case. E2 has every rational if k=2.
Classify the remaining k. A nonzero rational coefficient has a unique rational quotient. E2 has one rational solution for k≠2.
Cross-check the exceptional parameters. Each category must be evaluated in the original pair. At k=−6: E1 every, E2 one. At k=2: E1 none, E2 every.

grade9v3:analysis.stable_crux_move: Classify with a coupled domain boundary

questions.stem: Extension beyond routine linear equations. k is real, x must be rational. Classify the simultaneous system by k as INVALID PARAMETER, NO RATIONAL SOLUTION, ONE RATIONAL SOLUTION, or EVERY RATIONAL SOLUTION: (k−1)(k−2)x=k−1 and (x+1)/(x−1)=k/(k−2). An equation with a zero denominator is invalid; a solution must satisfy both original equations and x≠1. Report categories and the parameter cases, not a general numerical solution method.
conditions: Original calibration practice; independent educational review pending.
Advanced parameter/domain extension; not an ordinary Grade 9 retrieval question.

answer.summary: ONE RATIONAL SOLUTION at k=1; INVALID PARAMETER at k=2; NO RATIONAL SOLUTION for every other real k; never EVERY.
reasoning: Exclude the parameter making the second equation undefined. Its right denominator k−2 must be nonzero. k=2 is INVALID PARAMETER.
Isolate the zero-factor case k=1. The first equation then reads 0=0, while the second remains defined. The second becomes (x+1)/(x−1)=−1, giving x=0; it is rational and allowed.
Reduce the first equation for k outside {1,2}. Only in this branch is cancellation of k−1 followed by division by k−2 valid. x=1/(k−2).
Reduce the second equation with both denominator conditions retained. Cross-multiplication is reversible when x≠1 and k≠2. (k−2)(x+1)=k(x−1), hence x=k−1.
Require the two candidates to coincide. Both original equations must hold for the same x. (k−1)(k−2)=1, hence k²−3k+1=0.
Use the rational-domain restriction. The only compatibility parameters (3±√5)/2 are irrational; x=k−1 is then irrational and excluded. No rational solution for every k outside {1,2}.

Verify the exceptional allowed branch in the originals. A reduced-line result is insufficient when divisions were used in other branches. k=1,x=0 gives 0=0 and 1/(−1)=1/(−1). ONE at k=1; INVALID at k=2; NONE otherwise; never EVERY.

grade9v3:analysis.stable_crux_move: Execute an inverse chain across a table and a process graph

questions.stem: A measuring program uses numerical readings in centimetres: X → A=(X−1)/2 → B=3A+4 → C=(B+2)/5. The observation table gives C=22 millimetres. The inverse procedure is prescribed: convert the observation to centimetres, undo the C operation, then B, then A. Execute it to recover X and verify every forward stage. Treat the displayed readings as exact.
conditions: Original calibration practice; independent educational review pending.

reasoning: Convert the exact observation. Ten millimetres are one centimetre. C=22/10=11/5 centimetres.
Undo C=(B+2)/5. Multiplication by nonzero 5 and subtraction of 2 reverse this stage. B=5C−2=9.
Undo B=3A+4. Subtract 4, then divide by nonzero 3. A=(9−4)/3=5/3.
Undo A=(X−1)/2. Multiply by nonzero 2, then add 1. X=2(5/3)+1=13/3 centimetres.
Run the entire forward chain. A correct recovered input must reproduce the original observation after every named operation. 13/3 → 5/3 → 9 → 11/5 centimetres = 22 millimetres.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Ten millimetres are one centimetre.
inputs: A measuring program uses numerical readings in centimetres: X → A=(X−1)/2 → B=3A+4 → C=(B+2)/5. The observation table gives C=22 millimetres. The inverse procedure is prescribed: convert the observation to centimetres, undo the C operation, then B, then A. Execute it to recover X and verify every forward stage. Treat the displayed readings as exact.

reasoning_route.why_valid: Multiplication by nonzero 5 and subtraction of 2 reverse this stage.
Subtract 4, then divide by nonzero 3.
Multiply by nonzero 2, then add 1.
A correct recovered input must reproduce the original observation after every named operation.

answer.check: The forward chain gives A=5/3, B=9, C=11/5 cm =22 mm, so neither a unit mistake nor a reversed-step mistake survives the check.

hints.text: Keep the observation unit separate from the program unit.
Map each graph letter to its defining operation before substituting a number.
Start with the prescribed unit conversion, then apply the inverse steps in the given order. Leave the arithmetic and final reading to your attempt.

family_exposure.closure: Use C=20 mm. Expected X=11/3 cm; the forward chain gives 2 cm.

difficulty.basis: The governing procedure and inverse order are supplied, so execution is primary. The millimetre table must become a centimetre reading, the graph aliases must be tracked backward, and three dependent operations checked; representation 2, chain 2, algebra 1, unit/undo sensitivity 1 total 6.

independent_check.statement: The forward chain gives A=5/3, B=9, C=11/5 cm =22 mm, so neither a unit mistake nor a reversed-step mistake survives the check.

questions.stem: Over the reals, an author concludes x=4 from 2x=8 by dividing both sides by 2. Supply one warrant explaining why the conclusion follows and why the same justification would fail for division by zero. No further equation solving is requested.
conditions: Original calibration practice; independent educational review pending.

answer.summary: Because 2 is nonzero, dividing both sides by 2 is defined and reversible, preserving equality and the solution set. Division by zero is undefined.
reasoning: State the divisor property. The given divisor 2 is nonzero. Division by 2 is defined.
Connect the operation to its inverse. Multiplying both sides back by 2 restores the same equality. The step is reversible and preserves the solution set, establishing x=4.
Challenge the zero-divisor boundary. Division by zero is undefined, so it has no reversible operation of this kind. The warrant cannot license division by zero.
